newsitem.title: PERU: Peru says will go on talking to rebels.
newsitem.headline: Peru says will go on talking to rebels.

text.p: The Peruvian government on Tuesday decried "terrorist blackmail" by Marxist guerrillas holding 74 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima but said it would continue contact with the rebels to try and end the three-week-old standoff without bloodshed.
"We maintain a firm position of not giving in to blackmail from the terrorists," President Alberto Fujimori told reporters during a surprise visit to a Lima shantytown.
He said he hoped for a peaceful solution to the crisis and said the "physical well-being" of the hostages was assured "because there are not going to be acts of blood."

His prime minister, Alberto Pandolfi, said later that the government would continue "unofficial dealings" with the rebels of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), who seized the residence Dec. 17 during a diplomatic reception.
"The council of ministers has agreed to continue, in a timely way, the unofficial dealings towards reaching a global solution to the problem," Pandolfi said in a statement.

He said these dealings -- led so far by Education Minister Domingo Palermo -- were aimed at "exhausting all possible means for achieving a peaceful solution guaranteeing the physical integrity of those people kidnapped in the residence of the Japanese ambassador."

He did not say when Palermo would return to the residence, where he has not been seen for more than a week. His absence had prompted the rebels to say initial talks had been broken off by the government.

Fujimori, who ended his regular visits to shantytowns when the crisis began, said his trip was intended to show the world that life continued as normal in Peru despite the MRTA's takeover of the residence. "We should not transmit the image that in Peru we are living a situation of terrorism," he said.

Asked for his current stand in the crisis, he said: "A mixture of firmness in our position -- and in this sense the non-liberation of MRTA prisoners -- and at the same time prudence." The rebels have demanded from the outset that the government free all of their roughly 400 jailed comrades.
During a tour of the city's outskirts, Fujimori also visited a jail, passing by a wing holding MRTA members.

At around 3 p.m. (2000 GMT), a reporter and his interpeter working for a subsidiary of Japanese television station Asahi entered the residence at the invitation of the MRTA after sneaking into the compound through an adjoining house.

They left about two hours later, only to be arrested and driven away by anti-terrorism police to their headquarters in downtown Lima, where their notebooks and camera were confiscated. Asahi TV named them as Peruvian interpreter Victor Borja and New York-based reporter Tsuyoshi Hitomi.
Their entry into the residence, as well as that on New Year's Eve by a bigger group of journalists, was condemned by Pandolfi as "damaging to the seriousness and fluidity of talks."
Japanese diplomats in Lima also criticised them, saying their action was "extremely deplorable".

Earlier, an MRTA fighter fired two shots into the air shortly before dawn, shattering the edgy peace around the residence in the upscale San Isidro district. Two guerrillas slipped out of the building toward cars in the driveway, then fired a warning salvo as they went back inside, witnesses said.

Police surrounding the residence moved to a state of alert and speculated the MRTA was trying to make its presence felt. "We think it was a psychological tactic to let us know that they're there," one policeman said.
Red Cross spokesman Jean-Pierre Sharer later confirmed the shots were outside the house and there were no injuries to the hostages, who spent the morning writing letters to families.
The explosions underscored the delicately balanced nature of the crisis.

A series of hostage releases in which the guerrillas have freed more than 430 of their original captives stopped on New Year's Day. An MRTA spokesman said on Monday they would release no more until the two sides sat down to negotiate.
The rebels, who possess automatic rifles and grenade launchers, have mined and booby-trapped the residence in anticipation of an assault by government forces.
A report by local radio on Tuesday said security forces had captured in the central jungle an MRTA "military leader" but this could not be immediately confirmed with police.

Carlos Dario Perez was detained in the Chanchamayo Valley, a zone 220 miles (350 km) east of Lima, where the MRTA is believed to have bases, according to Cadena Peruana de Noticias radio. It gave no other details.
